title: Methodology
text:
This project examines the World Bank Group’s financing relationship with Costa Rica from 1980 to 2025. The central question is how that relationship evolved across four decades — in scale, instruments, sectoral priorities, and stated development objectives — and what the evolution reveals about the intersection of Costa Rica’s development trajectory and the World Bank Group’s changing institutional practice.
The analysis is explicitly not a causal study. It does not test whether World Bank lending caused changes in GDP, inequality, health, or other outcomes. It examines the portfolio itself and the context in which it operated.
Unit of analysis: Individual projects and loans, aggregated by year, period, and sector.
Geographic scope: Costa Rica only. Findings are not representative of the World Bank Group’s global portfolio or of developing-country experience generally.
Study period: 1980–2025 inclusive. Pre-1980 records are retained for reference but excluded from primary totals and charts. Three projects approved in 2025 are included. Records from 2026 are outside scope.

The Projects & Operations List supersedes the API as the authoritative project catalogue. The API-only extract used in earlier phases of this project omitted 43 projects, including the $420 million P148435 health insurance loan (2016).

title: Methodology
text:
3. Project universe reconciliation
The Projects & Operations List contains 115 Costa Rica project records. The IBRD Statement contains 68 loan records for 59 unique project IDs. The WB Projects API V2 extract contains 72 project records.



Membership
Count




All three sources (Projects List + API + loans)
51


Projects List + API (no loan record)
21


Projects List + loans (not in API)
8


Projects List only
35



The 43 projects in the Projects List but not in the API fall into four categories: 1. Legacy P006xxx-numbered projects not indexed in the V2 API search system (pre-2000). 2. Grants, GEF trust-fund operations, and other non-IBRD financing types. 3. Early-1990s IBRD loans not returned by the API. 4. P148435 ($420M, 2016) — the most significant missing project.
For IBRD financial analysis, only the 59 project IDs with loan records are used. Projects Board Approved but without loan records, and grants or trust funds, are excluded from financial totals.

title: Methodology
text:
4. Treatment of project approval dates
The V2 API extract had missing boardapprovaldate for 16 projects. A three-stage date recovery process was conducted:








Stage
Method
Outcome




Phase 0
V2 API extract
16 projects with NULL boardapprovaldate


Phase 1
V3 API + WB bulk Excel (downloaded 2026-10-30)
15/16 dates recovered; V3 and Excel agreed on all 15


Final
Projects & Operations List as primary source
Board dates used from Projects List where available



The one permanently unresolved project is P169724 (Learning for All, Dropped, $100 million planned). There is no approval date in any source for this project; it was likely never board-approved.
All recovered and original dates are compared against the Projects & Operations List. Where dates differ between sources, the Projects List is used as authoritative.

title: Methodology
text:
5. IBRD financial definitions
All IBRD amounts are from the IBRD Statement of Loans and Guarantees, snapshot 09/30/2026.







Term
Definition




Original Principal Amount
Loan amount as approved by the IBRD Board, in nominal US dollars at time of approval


Cancelled Amount
Portions of the principal cancelled — unused balances at close, mid-project reductions, or full cancellation of Terminated loans


Net Principal
original_principal - cancelled_amount. Represents the commitment net of cancellations. Not “money received.”


Undisbursed Amount
Remaining balance not drawn, converted at end-period exchange rate


Disbursed Amount
Cumulative drawdowns since inception. Not an annual flow. Cannot be assigned to approval year.


Repaid to IBRD
Cumulative principal repaid


Due to IBRD
Outstanding principal




Primary analytical measure
Original Principal Amount is used as the primary measure of approved lending scale. It maps cleanly to the approval year, is unambiguous (it was set at the board meeting), and allows comparison across time. Net principal is reported alongside it but not used as the primary measure for trend charts.
Real amounts use the formula: real_2025 = nominal * (defl_2025 / defl_approval_year), where defl_x is the World Bank GDP deflator value (NY.GDP.DEFL.ZS) for year x.


Cumulative disbursements and annual flows
The disbursed amounts in the IBRD Statement are cumulative balances as of 09/30/2026. They cannot be assigned to the approval year and do not represent annual disbursement flows. Annual disbursement data would require transaction-level records from the World Bank’s International Debt Statistics (IDS) or equivalent sources, which are not part of the current dataset.


Cancellations
Three loans have “Terminated” status: P006945, P006942, P006940. For these, original principal equals cancelled amount (net = 0); they were approved but the loan agreements were never signed or the loans never became effective. They are included in project counts but excluded from net principal totals.

title: Methodology
text:
6. Instrument classification
IBRD loan types in the Statement (CPL, FSL, NPL, SCL, SCPD) are financial-term codes, not operational instrument types. Classification as Development Policy Loan or Investment Project Financing uses the following logic, applied in 03_prepare_ibrd.R:







Classified as DPL
Reason




P006919, P006922, P006923, P006927, P006952
Structural Adjustment Loans (SAL I, II, III) or SAL-era policy lending


P111926 (CAT DDO, 2008)
Contingent credit line (DDO = deferred drawdown, policy-based)


P115173 (2009)
“Public Finance and Competitiveness Development Policy Loan”


P171912, P174786, P177029 (2020–2023)
“Fiscal and Decarbonization Management DPL”


P179861 (2023)
“Second Disaster Risk Management Development Policy Loan”


P181372 (2024)
“Social Risk Management DPL DDO”


P508347 (2025)
“Fiscal Management and Green Growth” — confirmed DPL in project description



All other projects are classified as Investment Project Financing. The NPL code (one loan) maps directly to DPL/adjustment.
Note: Several 1980s-era projects (P006933 Technical Assistance, P006924 Atlantic Agriculture, P006926 Transport Sector, P006938 Basic Education, P006941 Water Supply, P006954 Health Sector) had supplemental SCPD companion loans — a “policy tranche” common in the SAL era — but are classified as Investment Project Financing because the primary CPL loan funded investment activity. Only the pure SAL/structural adjustment operations are classified as DPL.

title: Methodology
text:
7. Sector classification
Sector information comes from two sources: 1. WB Projects API V2 (sector1, sector2, sector3 with name and percentage) 2. Projects & Operations List (Sector 1, 2, 3 — name only, no percentages)
API sector data is preferred; Projects List names supplement where API is unavailable.
Where sector percentages are available, project financing is allocated proportionally across sectors. For example, a $100M project with Sector 1 at 60% and Sector 2 at 40% contributes $60M and $40M respectively to sector totals. This avoids double-counting.
Limitation: Sector data is available for 22 of 35 in-scope IBRD projects. The 2020–2025 DPL series lacks sector percentage data in the API, significantly understating the financial weight of those operations in the sector analysis.
Ten broad sector groups are defined in functions.R:group_sector().

title: Methodology
text:
8. Inflation adjustment
Primary index: US GDP deflator, indicator NY.GDP.DEFL.ZS, retrieved from World Bank API (api.worldbank.org/v2/country/US/indicator/NY.GDP.DEFL.ZS).
Base year: 2020 = 100 (as returned by the API).
Coverage: 1960–2025, no missing years.
Why GDP deflator (not CPI): CPI measures consumer price changes affecting US households; the GDP deflator measures price changes across all US-produced final goods and services. For comparing the real scale of historical dollar-denominated financial commitments, the GDP deflator is more appropriate.
Limitations: - Neither index measures the local purchasing power of lending in Costa Rica. - The 2025 deflator value is preliminary and may be revised in future WB data vintages. - A $100M loan in 1985 purchased different quantities of Costa Rican infrastructure than $100M in 2020.
Validation: The 1980→2025 multiplier is approximately 3.275, consistent with the Phase 1 reference check (~$328M in 2025 USD per $100M in 1980).

title: Methodology
text:
9. IFC methodology
IFC investment amounts represent IFC’s own-account investment in private entities and are fundamentally different from IBRD sovereign loan principal. They are never combined with IBRD figures.
Date caveat: Only 2 IFC projects (Advisory Services) have actual Approval Date values. All Investment projects show Projected Board Date — a planned date, not an actual approval confirmation. Year assignments from IFC data are approximate and should not be used for precise annual time-series claims.
Amount parsing: The Investment as Approved by The Board field in the IFC Excel contains text such as “15.0 million (USD)…”. Investment amounts are extracted by parsing the leading number.
Deduplication: The source file contains 40 rows for 30 unique project numbers (10 projects have multiple disclosure documents). The final dataset uses one row per project number, taking the first non-missing value for each field.
Known issues documented in 04_prepare_ifc.R: BAC CR Green ($200M, 2025), Coopenae ($15M, 2011), Aeropuerto Juan Santamaría ($35M, 2000), Corporacion Supermercados Unidos ($40M, multi-country), Insulet CR ($97M, pipeline/excluded).

title: Methodology
text:
10. MIGA methodology
MIGA Gross Exposure Up to represents the maximum possible MIGA liability under issued guarantee contracts, not a loan or capital transfer.
Fiscal year: MIGA uses World Bank fiscal years (July 1 – June 30). FY2008 = July 2007 – June 2008.
Deduplication: Project 3639 (Grupo del Istmo de Papagayo) appears three times in the source data (FY2001, FY2002, FY2003) with amounts of $16.4M, $38.3M, and $81M respectively. These represent successive disclosure events for the same development, not three independent guarantees. The FY2001 and FY2002 rows are removed; FY2003 ($81M) is used as the canonical record representing peak exposure. Summing all three rows would overstate by ~$136M.

title: Methodology
text:
11. IDA context
Costa Rica’s last IDA credit was in FY1962 (source: World Bank IDA Graduates page). The 1980–2025 analysis is entirely IBRD. The IBRD Statement contains no IDA transactions for Costa Rica.

title: Methodology
section: 12. Calendar year vs fiscal year conventions
text:
12. Calendar year vs fiscal year conventions
IBRD and the Projects & Operations List use calendar-year board approval dates. IFC and MIGA use World Bank fiscal years (July–June). This project uses calendar years for the primary IBRD analysis. IFC and MIGA dates are labelled as approximate or fiscal-year as appropriate.

title: Methodology
text:
14. Reproducibility
The complete analysis can be rebuilt from raw source files.
Prerequisites: R ≥ 4.4, Quarto ≥ 1.4, R packages listed in R/00_setup.R.
Pipeline (run in order from project root):
source("R/06_prepare_wdi.R")    # deflator and WDI (requires internet)
source("R/01_import_sources.R") # documentation only
source("R/02_reconcile_projects.R")
source("R/03_prepare_ibrd.R")
source("R/04_prepare_ifc.R")
source("R/05_prepare_miga.R")
source("R/07_analysis.R")
source("R/08_visualizations.R")
source("R/09_validation.R")     # all checks should pass
Then render the site:
quarto render
Scripts requiring internet access: 06_prepare_wdi.R (World Bank API calls for deflator and WDI indicators). All other scripts read from data/raw/ only.
Raw files in data/raw/ must be preserved unchanged. The archive/ directory contains historical exploratory scripts from Phase 0 and Phase 1; they are not part of the active pipeline.

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
text:
Costa Rica is a small Central American country with an outsized reputation. By the early 2000s, it had achieved life-expectancy figures comparable to the United States, nearly universal health coverage, and internationally recognised environmental leadership — despite a per-capita income that placed it firmly in the middle of the middle-income range. It abolished its military in 1948. It pioneered payments for ecosystem services. It built human capital while other countries were building armies.
And yet, across the same forty-five years, it borrowed heavily from the World Bank.
This project examines that relationship — not as a straightforward story of aid and development, but as an evolving institutional relationship between a country’s changing needs and strategy and a lender’s changing priorities and instruments.
Between 1980 and 2025, the World Bank’s IBRD approved 35 loans to Costa Rica with an original principal of $4.6B in nominal US dollars — or $6.2B in constant 2025 dollars. Over the same period, the Bank’s private-sector arm (IFC) made approximately $874 million in own-account investments in Costa Rican private enterprises, and its guarantee agency (MIGA) issued historical guarantees with a total peak exposure of approximately $336 million.
The character of that engagement changed substantially across four decades — from structural adjustment and crisis response in the 1980s, to targeted investment in health, education, infrastructure, and environment in the 1990s and 2000s, to large-scale policy-based lending for fiscal reform and decarbonization in the 2020s. Understanding those changes — and what drove them — is the central analytical task.

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
text:
Costa Rica is a small Central American country with an outsized reputation. By the early 2000s, it had achieved life-expectancy figures comparable to the United States, nearly universal health coverage, and internationally recognised environmental leadership — despite a per-capita income that placed it firmly in the middle of the middle-income range. It abolished its military in 1948. It pioneered payments for ecosystem services. It built human capital while other countries were building armies.
And yet, across the same forty-five years, it borrowed heavily from the World Bank.
This project examines that relationship — not as a straightforward story of aid and development, but as an evolving institutional relationship between a country’s changing needs and strategy and a lender’s changing priorities and instruments.
Between 1980 and 2025, the World Bank’s IBRD approved 35 loans to Costa Rica with an original principal of $4.6B in nominal US dollars — or $6.2B in constant 2025 dollars. Over the same period, the Bank’s private-sector arm (IFC) made approximately $874 million in own-account investments in Costa Rican private enterprises, and its guarantee agency (MIGA) issued historical guarantees with a total peak exposure of approximately $336 million.
The character of that engagement changed substantially across four decades — from structural adjustment and crisis response in the 1980s, to targeted investment in health, education, infrastructure, and environment in the 1990s and 2000s, to large-scale policy-based lending for fiscal reform and decarbonization in the 2020s. Understanding those changes — and what drove them — is the central analytical task.

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
text:
The institutions involved
The World Bank Group is not a single institution. It comprises five related organisations.
IBRD (International Bank for Reconstruction and Development) lends to creditworthy middle-income governments at near-market rates. Costa Rica has been an IBRD borrower throughout the study period and is the main subject of this analysis.
IDA (International Development Association) provides concessional financing to the poorest countries. Costa Rica’s last IDA credit was in FY1962. The 1980–2025 analysis is entirely IBRD.
IFC (International Finance Corporation) invests in private-sector entities — banks, agribusinesses, manufacturers, utilities. IFC does not lend to governments. Its investments in Costa Rica are analysed separately as a companion to the IBRD story.
MIGA (Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency) issues political-risk guarantees to private investors. MIGA’s financial measure — gross exposure — is the maximum potential liability under the guarantee, not a loan or disbursement. MIGA has been active in Costa Rica’s tourism, banking, and infrastructure sectors.
ICSID provides investment dispute arbitration and is not a financing institution.

These financial measures are not comparable. IBRD original principal, IFC own-account investment, and MIGA gross exposure each represent different instruments and different kinds of financial exposure. They cannot be summed.

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
text:
Four decades of IBRD lending





Annual IBRD commitments to Costa Rica, 1980–2025. Darker bars show nominal USD; lighter bars show the same amounts in constant 2025 USD using the US GDP deflator. The 2022 bar shows a net negative from a Terminated loan (P178320).




The IBRD lending record reveals four broadly distinguishable periods:

The 1980s: Crisis response and structural adjustment
The 1980s opened with the worst economic crisis Costa Rica had experienced since independence. Between 1979 and 1982, GDP fell by nearly 10%, inflation reached 90%, and the country defaulted on its external debt. The World Bank’s response — coordinated with the IMF and USAID — was a series of Structural Adjustment Loans: SAL I (1985), SAL II (1988), SAL III (1993), and their companion Technical Assistance and Export Development loans.
These loans were policy-based: money in exchange for specific economic policy changes — trade liberalisation, public-sector reform, reduction in state-owned enterprise activity, deregulation. In real 2025 dollars, the 1980s saw $772M in total commitments, approximately 80% of it in policy-based instruments.
The structural adjustment programme was controversial. It reshaped Costa Rica’s development model, accelerating the shift from import-substitution industrialisation toward export-oriented manufacturing and services. Whether those changes improved welfare — and for whom — remains actively debated.


The 1990s and 2000s: Investment lending and diversification
After the adjustment era, IBRD lending shifted toward targeted investments: the Ecomarkets payment-for-ecosystem-services project (2000), health sector strengthening (2001), education equity (2005), environmental mainstreaming (2006), and port-city infrastructure in Limón (2008). A CAT-DDO contingency credit in 2008 provided a disaster-risk buffer.
The 2009 $500 million Public Finance and Competitiveness DPL-DDO was the largest single World Bank commitment to Costa Rica in the entire 1980–2025 period — extended as the global financial crisis threatened Costa Rica’s fiscal position. It was development policy lending, but triggered not by structural reform conditionality as in the 1980s, but by an economic emergency.


The 2010s: Sustained but concentrated investment
The 2010s saw only two IBRD projects: the $200 million Higher Education Improvement loan (2012) and — crucially, and previously missing from this project’s earlier analysis — the $420 million Strengthening Universal Health Insurance loan (2016), supporting the Caja Costarricense del Seguro Social (CCSS). This was the largest investment-type operation in the portfolio. Its prior absence from the analysis was a significant error.


The 2020s: The DPL surge and the fiscal-climate nexus
The period 2020–2025 accounts for 57.9% of all nominal 1980–2025 commitments — twelve projects, $2.66 billion. Several forces converged: the COVID-19 crisis, Costa Rica’s long-building fiscal consolidation (the 2018 fiscal reform was a turning point), and the country’s articulation of a Decarbonization Plan. The Bank’s response was a series of large DPLs tying fiscal reform to climate targets.
This pattern — fiscal policy and environmental policy fused into a single lending instrument — is new in the portfolio. It reflects both the Bank’s institutional evolution toward “green” conditionality and Costa Rica’s own strategic positioning of its environmental identity.





Instrument mix by period. Policy-based lending dominated the 1980s, virtually disappeared in the 2010s, and returned at scale in the 2020s.

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
text:
Sectoral priorities





Sectoral composition of allocated commitments. Sector data is available for 22 of 35 in-scope projects; recent approvals without sector percentages are excluded.




The sector picture is necessarily incomplete — sector percentage data is unavailable for several large recent loans, including the 2020–2025 DPL series, which describe their operations in terms of policy pillars rather than traditional sectors. Where data is available, the portfolio shows:

Transportation and infrastructure dominated early lending (roads, power, ports).
Finance and public administration grew through the SAL era and the 2000s fiscal reform.
Education and health appeared as persistent investment targets across multiple periods.
Agriculture, forestry, and environment formed a sustained thread, from the Ecomarkets PES scheme to the sustainable fisheries project.

The 2020s DPL series defies easy sector classification. Their stated objectives span fiscal management, climate policy, social protection, and energy transition simultaneously — a reflection of how policy-based lending increasingly integrates multiple development domains.





Thematic language in project abstracts, by period. Environment and climate are present in every period, but the vocabulary shifts.

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
text:
Development context





Costa Rica’s development trajectory. These are contextual patterns, not evidence that World Bank lending caused the observed changes.




Costa Rica’s economic and social trajectory over the period is striking. GDP per capita grew from approximately $2,000 in 1980 to $18,900 in 2024 — an increase that survived structural adjustment, two regional crises, the global financial crisis, and the COVID pandemic. Life expectancy rose from 73 years to 80.8 years.
Whether World Bank lending contributed to these improvements — or was merely present alongside them — cannot be established from this evidence. What the data does show is that the largest lending episodes (the 1985 SAL series, the 2009 DPL-DDO, the 2016 health loan, the 2020–2025 DPL series) coincided with specific economic stresses or strategic priorities, rather than tracking smoothly with GDP growth or development outcomes.
The Gini index shows a more complicated picture: moderate inequality with some improvement in the 2010s, followed by a COVID-era spike.

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
text:
IFC: private-sector finance





IFC own-account investments in Costa Rica by indicative board date and sector. Amounts in nominal USD. Not comparable to IBRD sovereign lending.




IFC has made 23 investments in Costa Rica (as of the disclosure record), with total own-account investment of approximately $874 million (nominal USD, indicative). The portfolio is overwhelmingly concentrated in financial services — commercial banks, SME lenders, housing finance institutions. The second-largest sector is energy, led by the $100 million Reventazon hydroelectric project (2012), the largest hydroelectric facility in Central America.
Several observations are important:

IFC board dates in this dataset are projected (planned), not confirmed actual approval dates. Year assignments are approximate.
The $200 million BAC Costa Rica Green (2025) includes a $30 million unfunded guarantee line; IFC’s own investment is $200 million.
The pending Insulet CR project ($97 million, 2026) is excluded from historical totals.
IFC amounts cannot be compared with IBRD sovereign loan principal or summed into a “World Bank Group total.”

The IFC portfolio reflects a different dimension of the Bank’s engagement: not sovereign policy conditionality, but private capital mobilisation in a middle-income country with a functioning financial sector.

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
text:
MIGA: political risk guarantees
Between 1995 and 2008, MIGA issued guarantees on 10 Costa Rica projects (deduplicated) across tourism, banking, power, transportation, and manufacturing. The total peak gross exposure was approximately $336 million.
MIGA guarantees protect foreign investors against political risks such as transfer restriction, expropriation, and contract breach. They represent a different kind of institutional engagement: not lending, but de-risking private investment decisions.
The largest MIGA guarantee was $158.5 million for the Autopistas del Sol toll road (FY2008), reflecting the Bank Group’s support for private infrastructure investment at the same time as the IBRD was extending a fiscal DPL.

title: The World Bank Group in Costa Rica
section: What the evidence shows — and what it does not
text:
What the evidence shows — and what it does not
What the data shows:

The World Bank’s IBRD has been a persistent, but not dominant, source of external financing for Costa Rica since the early 1980s.
The character of IBRD engagement shifted substantially across periods: adjustment lending in the 1980s, project investment in the 1990s–2000s, large-scale policy loans in the 2020s.
Development policy lending and investment lending alternated in dominance, responding to specific economic conditions and strategic moments.
Environmental and climate themes appear in every period but in different forms — from discrete conservation projects to comprehensive fiscal-climate policy packages.
The $420 million health insurance loan (2016) is the single largest investment-type operation in the portfolio and was previously absent from this project’s analysis due to an API data gap.
IFC investment in Costa Rica is substantial and concentrated in finance, consistent with IFC’s mandate in creditworthy middle-income countries.

What the data cannot show:

Whether World Bank lending caused improvements in GDP, health, or social indicators.
Whether policy conditionality shaped Costa Rica’s development trajectory or merely ratified decisions the government had already made.
Whether the absence of Bank lending in certain years reflected Bank disengagement, Costa Rica’s own financing preferences, or fiscal conditions that made borrowing unattractive.
The direction of influence: did Costa Rica’s environmental agenda attract Bank support, or did Bank support amplify an agenda Costa Rica would have pursued regardless?

These questions are interesting precisely because the evidence cannot resolve them from a single country’s loan record. They are questions for the next phase of research.

See the EDA & Analysis page for charts and tables, the Methodology page for source documentation, and the Data Dictionary for variable definitions.

Project 3639 (Grupo del Istmo de Papagayo) appeared in FY2001, FY2002, and FY2003 with escalating cumulative exposures ($16.4M, $38.3M, $81M).
